Madam Speaker, I thought I might ask the same question that I asked of the member for Egmont of the member for Burin-St. George's.
He will remember that in 1977 the Liberal government cut funding to the provinces with the end of block funding. In 1982, with the end of the revenue guarantee program, there was a further cut to the provinces of some $6 billion. In 1983, the six-and-five restraints ended up by reducing contributions to the provinces by almost $.5 billion.
I wonder if the hon. member could indicate why- since the member for Egmont was not prepared to-the cuts are so terrible when the Conservatives make them, but they are not so terrible when the Liberals make them when they are in power.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing for the question. When he put it to my colleague, the hon. member for Egmont-and I knew that he would do a good job of answering it, as he did-I found myself rather enviously saying: "If only I got a question like that". I really did not ask him to ask the question. I have to tell you that, Madam Speaker, to start with. I thank him anyway.
The answer is very simple. The answer, first of all, is that a member from a party, which has never been the government and never will be, would not be able to appreciate that sometimes in a government you do tailor, you do make changes. Sometimes you get a signal from the people that enough is enough.
Is his real question: "What distinguishes the Liberals from the Tories?" The NDPers, the arm-chair socialists-if they had to be real socialists they would be in real trouble-can afford to be socialists because they are getting half-decent salaries. If they ever formed the government, they would find this out. In the meantime, they are getting nervous about their place in the polls.
You will notice, Madam Speaker, what is happening. Every day 85 per cent of the country are out there railing at this government. Yet what are members of the NDP doing? They are wondering who is going to have the mate's chair on the Titanic. They are fighting over Titanic chairs, when they ought to be representing the people in an attack on this government. They are elbowing for
Government Orders
room over here because they are worried that we might elbow them out somehow.
I say to him, a man who will never be in government unless he has the good sense to apply for admission to this particular caucus-and we would consider the application because he is a fairly bright fellow-the answer is this. Here is the difference. He is going around telling the country that the Liberals and the Tories are Tweedledum and Tweedledee. When we in 1972 and on other dates began to do things that were not particularly unpopular, we got the message. This crowd does not know how to get the message.
I submit that one of the most fundamental principles of our kind of government, our kind of parliamentary democracy, is, yes, we provide leadership as a government, but you never force leadership down people's throats. You never say to them: "This is medicine. It is nasty but it is going to be good for you". The patient, the country as a whole, must want the medicine.
They said on GST, they said on EPF: "We do not want this medicine". They said it to us in 1977 and 1982 and we heard them. That is the difference between a Liberal and a Tory.
If you want to know the difference between a Tory and an NDPer, one gets into government once in a while, the other one never.

Madam Speaker, the member for Burin-St. George's in Newfoundland made an excellent presentation. In fact, because the government of Brian Mulroney was elected in 1984 we in fact helped to share in the rest of Canada. We sent to many parts of Canada, through a Progressive Conservative government, some really positive things.
For example, in Newfoundland since 1984 we have created 29,000 new jobs. That compares to the 1,000 that were lost while the member who spoke was in office. Unemployment has fallen by 14,000 in that same

five-year period. While he was in office prior to 1984 it rose by 25,000. The list goes on.

Does he believe that all people in Canada should share in the challenge of dealing with the deficit, or just those who for his logic come from Ontario?

Madam Speaker, I thank the member for Ontario because just as I thought he was going to be completely selective in his quotation of statistics, he half redeemed himself. He was only half selective. He did come so close as to talk about the deficit. He conveniently forgot the public debt. I wonder why.
Let us give him the benefit of the doubt. Let us say that he forgot. For the sake of the House and in the interest of time I will say what he would have said.
He would surely have pointed out that the public debt when the Tories took over in 1984 was of the order of $170 billion.
$160 billion.

First, when will he and others get the message, whether they are talking Meech Lake, EPF or about anything else concerning the way this country is fabricated and constructed? Either we believe in the equality of every voter in this country, regardless of where he or she lives, or we do not. We are sick and tired-as in stomachy, which is what we say back home- of having it rammed down our throats, just as the hon. member tried to do a minute ago again, that somehow we ought be eternally grateful with the few crumbs coming off the table.
When will the member get the message that we would like to be in a position to help buy the bread to put on the table? We would like to be sitting at the table. We would like to be full partners. Do not give me that patronizing nonsense. What we get in this country, we get as a right. We make no apologies to any man, woman or child in this country for that.
He says things are not destitute in Newfoundland. He ought to come down and visit. speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Resuming debate with the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing.
April 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, I rise today in support of the 80 per cent of Canadians who oppose the government's initiative in Bill C-69.
Of all the short-sighted, mean-spirited and counterproductive decisions by this government, of which there have been many of course, this current bill represents the worst. Not only will it cause needless human suffering today, as we experience cutbacks in our health care system, but if the government does not change its approach we will condemn our children to a life of mediocrity and ill-health, effectively reversing gains made by our parents and grandparents in building this country.
Let us be clear about what this Tory government is proposing to do. First, it is withdrawing from health care funding, thereby beginning the end of universal medicare and health insurance programs, thus threatening the future health of our children and the sick.
Second, it is withdrawing from post-secondary education, thereby condemning the next generation to lives of hewers of wood and drawers of water, and ensuring the slow decline of Canada in the ranks of the world's nations.
Just to illustrate the extent of the move away from supporting the provinces, the Library of Parliament's figures show that in the nine years from 1986-87 to 1994-95 this government's actions, including the actions in Bill C-69, will take almost $29 billion from the provinces in terms of health care and post-secondary education funding. These are massive cuts in support from the federal government to Canada's health care and post-secondary education system.
We have seen nurses' strikes. We have seen threatened doctors' strikes. We have seen long waiting lists for elective surgery. We have seen Canadians being turned away from hospitals and indeed dying through lack of care.
Canadians are worried, and justifiably so, by a tax on medicare, with the very real threat of one health care system for the rich and another for the poor.
The same goes for the post-secondary education system. Indeed, one eminent president of one of Canada's best universities recently wrote to me saying that our university system has experienced an outstanding fiscal
Government Orders
erosion in the past decade, the magnitude of which is unparalleled in any other Canadian public sector. The situation has become an embarrassment and a concern of monumental proportions.
Our share of the education and training budget for the last few years, according to recent StatsCanada figures, has reduced. Indeed, it is reduced in large measure by comparison to the percentage of Gross National Product. It has been reduced from 1.3 per cent, for example, in 1986-87, to 1.1 per cent in 1988-89. It is continuing to fall.
Total federal government spending, if you exclude the debt charges, rose by 3.6 per cent and 7.6 per cent respectively in 1987-1988 and 1988-1989. By contrast, spending on education rose by only 1.8 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively.
Clearly, the federal government's commitment to post-secondary education is reducing by comparison to its commitment to other expenditures in the budget.
Indeed, the increases in education spending are the lowest year over year increases on record, according to the government's own figures from StatsCanada.
In spite of the Prime Minister's rhetoric about social programs being a sacred trust, we have here a major cut to health care funding, Canada's most prized social program. It is little wonder that the Prime Minister's performance rating is only 19 per cent, the lowest of all Prime Ministers since polling started almost 50 years ago.
The Prime Minister has also made commitments about the importance of education and the role of the federal government in ensuring a first-class education system in Canada, and every Canadian's right to a world-class education. Then, immediately afterward, he slashed $10 million from the post-secondary education budget to the provinces over the next nine years.
We have heard a lot, too, about research and development. Indeed, two years ago a committee chaired by the Prime Minister, the National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, looked at research financing and recommended that it be doubled. Our scientists and scholars are operating with resources that continue to place them at a severe disadvantage when we compare them to others in the international community. Yet the proposal to double financing over three years has yet to be

April 23, 1990
Government Orders
implemented. In effect, there is no indication that it ever will be.
There is a national interest in post-secondary education and health care funding. That is why the federal government became involved in supporting the provinces in those two areas in the first place. There has been in the past a commitment to ensure that no matter where a person lives, no matter what a person's financial opportunities might be, they be entitled, as all Canadians are, to the same quality of health care and the same quality of post-secondary education.
Yet this government is either deliberately or recklessly saying there is no longer any public interest in ensuring equal accessibility, regardless of financial means or geographic location. The government is saying that there is no longer a need for health care, academic ability and being able to use education as the criteria by which we will choose those who can have access to health care and post-secondary education. What the government is doing is turning its back on years of development toward more equality in Canada.
No longer will a sick person in Atlantic Canada have the same opportunity for health care as a person in a richer province. No longer will a young person in Saskatchewan have the same educational opportunities as someone in a richer province.
As we all know, the bill attacks the poorer provinces, creating greater strains on federalism without apparent care for the consequences. Fully 70 per cent of the cuts proposed in this bill are in terms of health care, post-secondary education and the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan.
That means that this government's decision to deal with the deficit is to ensure that those who are sick, those who are young and in the process of being educated and the very poorest in our society are to bear the burden of attacking the deficit. Eighty per cent of Canadians have told this government not to follow this approach, but of course as with the goods and services tax, unemployment insurance, VIA Rail and so many other things the government has turned a blind eye and deaf ear to Canadians.
This is a strategy which will tear Canada apart. We cannot encourage tension between the regions. We cannot pit Saskatchewan against Atlantic Canada for our
resources in order to fund health care and post-secondary education. We cannot make it difficult for those in the poorer regions to experience what other Canadians experience.
What we have seen over the last few months is an increase in intolerance in this country and an increase in tension between the regions as a direct result of the government's actions. Bill C-69 is merely one example of that.
The government's approach is easy to predict. As a result of its general philosophy which is reflected in free trade and the goods and services tax, its approach is that the government should withdraw from the economy and that people should look out for themselves. If this means that those living in less well-off areas do without vital health care and post-secondary education services then, according to this government, so be it.
In some parts of our country, including my own province of Saskatchewan, provinces have very little tax room left to make up for reductions in money from the federal government. The effect is that the quality of programs in those provinces declines while better off provinces, such as Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta, are able to make up the difference through provincial taxes should they decide to do so.
That increase in regional disparity is something which those of us in the New Democratic Party not only criticize and oppose but know that most Canadians oppose it also.
In addition, we also oppose another thrust of what lies behind the government's actions under Bill C-69. That is with regard to privatization. There are many examples of supporters of the government, including the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and The Globe and Mail who argue for increased privatization both in the health care system and in the post-secondary education system. As for universities and colleges, there are something over 50 universities and colleges at the present time attempting to raise more than $1 billion in revenues to try to make up for some of the shortfalls from both federal and provincial governments.
The withdrawal of the federal government from educational funding is forcing both the gradual privatization of education with concomitant reductions in access and higher tuition fees across the country.
April 23, 1990

Madam Speaker, let me indicate two examples of the calls for privatization just to show that I am not being an alarmist but am indicating that there are many who are calling for this and that the government is responding. The National Citizens Coalition, for example, has argued that the government's monopoly of health care has resulted in inefficiency, cut-backs in services, medical rationing and that it has increased costs astronomically. According to it Canada's health care system needs a dose of competition. It also argues that the Canada health care system would benefit if the government contracted out the management of public hospitals. That is not what most Canadians want.
The nurses also have indicated that the pressure is growing on our medicare system. Indeed, they have argued that medicare is in trouble and that Canadians had better watch out if they want to have the sort of public health care system that we have grown accustomed to in Canada. Of course the federal government's actions under Bill C-69 and related actions in the past have contributed and caused the fears that I have mentioned.
In addition, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association has argued that Canadian universities should be deregulated and that Canadians are paying far too great a share of each student's education costs.
We are seeing pressures and hearing pressures on our health care system and on our post-secondary education system. Rather than respond to them by fighting back and by ensuring that our health and post-secondary systems are the best they can be, the government is giving into those pressures and cutting back on the funding to the provinces. This is having a particularly bad effect on those poor provinces, including the province of Saskatchewan.
The government's view of federal funding to the provinces under the Established Programs Financing arrangements, at least according to the Minister of Finance, appears to be that the moneys can be used by the provinces as they see fit. This is simply not the case.
The Canada Health Act and the Established Programs Financing arrangements are very closely linked, as the Canada Health Act clearly states. Indeed, in the past
Government Orders
both the Minister of Finance when he was in opposition, and other members of his party, have argued very strenuously-that was when the Liberals made cuts to these programs-that the Established Programs Financing arrangements were indeed arrangements which were designed to finance both health care and post-secondary education in the provinces. It seems to me that they cannot have it both ways. They cannot have said, when the Liberals were making cuts, that these cuts were to health and post-secondary education and now when they themselves are making cuts argue that they are for whatever purposes the provinces so desire.
To say that the provinces can do what they want with the money is to ignore the Canada Health Act. To say that, the federal government is not interested any longer in national standards of health care and post-secondary education, both in terms of quality of health care and post-secondary education and in terms of accessibility. As I said, that is not what the Minister of Finance and other Conservative ministers said when they were in opposition and the Liberals were making cuts to EPF.
In 1982, in the budget of then finance minister MacEa-chen, there was an elimination of the revenue guarantee. At the time the present Minister of Finance said that the Liberal minister was prepared to risk major cut-backs in medical care and post-secondary education and that he should not rush into these decisions on a unilateral basis and force spending cuts and service cuts on the provinces.
We all know that the provinces are not in agreement with the cuts that they are facing. We also know that these cuts will affect the services available at the provincial level. The present Minister of Finance said in 1982 that we should not cause closures of hospitals and cut-backs in post-secondary education in this way. The Minister of Finance has had a change of heart and now argues that these expenditures are not for health care and post-secondary education, whereas he quite clearly was of the view that they were in 1982.
Many other members on the government side spoke strenuously against the cuts which were proposed and, indeed, introduced by the Liberal government in 1982 and 1984 and, indeed, pointed out the opportunities

April 23, 1990
Government Orders
which were available to the provinces in the event of such cuts. There really are only four. The provinces can increase revenues if they have the opportunity to do so or they can increase their deficit. They can cut back or reduce services. It seems to me, as the Conservative member said, when faced with those Liberal cuts we really should not do that and, indeed, we cannot do that because of the danger that it will pose to Canadians across the country. The third alternative is to reduce standards of services and the fourth is merely for the provinces to increase taxation. None of those are attractive features and particularly for those provinces which are faced with difficulties in raising any more funds.
As I have raised in questions, I want to make just one brief mention on the fact that, when the Liberal government was in power up until 1984, it made a number of similar attacks on the health care system and on post-secondary education. Those attacks were not as great as those made by the Conservative government but, nonetheless, they indicate a lack of commitment to the health care system and post-secondary education system by Liberal governments of the time.
As I mentioned, in 1977, the end of block funding constituted cuts from the federal government to the provinces. In 1982, there was the removal of the revenue guarantee program which cut some $6 billion over a five-year period from federal transfers to the provinces and the six and five restraints in 1983 cut some $400 million to $500 million out of the education support programs for the provinces.
The irony of Progressive Conservatives and Liberals changing places is not lost on Canadians. When Liberals make cuts to transfers for health and post-secondary education, Progressive Conservative members correctly criticize, and when Progressive Conservative governments make cuts, the Liberals complain.
The Minister of Finance was right in 1982 when he said these cuts would adversely affect health care and postsecondary education across this country and he is wrong now when he says the provinces should be able to spend that money as they see fit. This government has lost track of the lives of ordinary, hard-working Canadians who rely on medicare and who want their children to have a good education. The regions, especially the less well-off provinces, will be devastated by this bill.
The maritime provinces already devote an enormous share of their provincial budgets to health and education costs. Cuts in federal spending will push them to the breaking point, as we have seen in Prince Edward Island, for example, with the provincial budget being pushed into deficit. In Prince Edward Island, health expenditure expressed as a percentage of gross domestic product was over 12 per cent as compared to only 8 per cent for Ontario. In other words, health expenditures make up 50 per cent more available financial resources in P.E.I. than in Ontario.
How will smaller provinces manage, given these cuts? How much less opportunity will they have to make up the cuts given the lack of fiscal base on which to raise other sources of tax revenue? As I have mentioned, the only alternatives are to increase taxes or increase the provincial deficit, or reduce services. None of those options are acceptable to Canadians.
In other words, as we have seen represented in many presentations and many reports, the government is creating a health care system for the rich and a health care system for the poor. It is creating a two-tier health care system, depending on whether you live in a rich province or a poor province, and it will do the same with regard to post-secondary education.
In closing, this government should stand up for the regions, stand up for the needs of Canadians in their health and post-secondary education systems. It should help, not hurt, which is what it is doing with Bill C-69. Government is about choices and this government has chosen the goods and services tax, it has chosen to give big tax write-offs to the rich and to corporations and it has chosen to attack health care and post-secondary education. No wonder the government is at 15 per cent in the polls. The final price, of course, will be paid at the next election.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to what was said by our colleague from the New Democratic Party, and I fully understood the message he was trying to get across. One wonders why, if the government across the way was listening, and I am sure the hon. member for Brampton was listening very carefully and that he will take to heart the points raised by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Clark's Crossing-I would like to ask him whether he was aware of the fact, for instance, that Bill C-69 intends to make budget cutbacks
April 23, 1990

totalling $110 billion this year, $1,780 billion next year and that, spread out over five years, these budgetary compressions will add up to about $8,380 billion.
Of course, my point is that all this will have a very negative impact on the provinces' ability to deal with the financial problems they will have as a result of the federal government's decisions. For instance, there is the impact that this budgetary restraint will have on welfare rates in the provinces, and so forth. I would like to tell him that, for instance, in my riding, in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, the federal government intends to use Bill C-21 to cut benefits to workers, which will cause an increase in the number of people on welfare, because people will exhaust their unemployment insurance benefits faster. So there will be an increase in the number of people on welfare, and at the same time, the federal government, which gives these funds to the provinces, is saying: Listen, we know you are going to have more welfare recipients, but we are cutting back just the same. Doesn't he agree that these cutbacks are entirely unreasonable and that, in fact, the government is not saving one cent? It is just passing the problem on to someone else.
[English ]

I am
not sure that the hon. member asked me a question, Madam Speaker, but that clearly is what is taking place with this particular bill, indeed with the general activities of the government surrounding the budget at the present time.
The budget has been described as a pass-the-buck budget and that clearly is what it does. It transfers the responsibility for dealing with the deficit from the federal government to the provincial governments. It chooses to attack health care programs, post-secondary education systems and the poorest of Canadians by its decision to put a cap on the Canada Assistance Program. That is the decision the government has made. That is not the choice or the decision the government had to make, it is the one it decided to make and Canadians, of course, will not forget that.
It is an unacceptable approach for the government to take in dealing with the deficit. No one, I think, is arguing that the deficit is something which should not be
Government Orders
attacked. We all agree, that the government has an obligation and that indeed we all have an obligation to deal with the deficit. The question is how we are going to deal with it. Are we going to deal with it by attacking those who are less well off in our society, are we going to deal with it by attacking those who have less opportunity to fight back, or are we going to do so by increasing the tax burden on the well-off and the corporations in Canada, for example, as well as doing such things as attacking interest rates?
The government, as we know, has chosen to attack the less well off and those who are less capable of protecting themselves. That is unacceptable. I do not think any of us on this side of the House would consider it to be acceptable and I do not think most Canadians think that it is acceptable.
As a final point of a more general nature, when we all go back to our ridings, I think we understand the way in which Canadians are responding to this attack on them by this government. One of the reasons for increased intolerance in our country, which I especially see when I go to the west-attacks on bilingualism and multicultur-alism on other parts of the country-is that people are fed up with being attacked by their government when they feel that their government should be helping them rather than kicking them.
The government just has to accept the responsibility for what it is doing to this country due to financial burdens being placed on the provinces with the increased cuts to health care funding and post-secondary education funding. It also has to accept the responsibility for the mood that it is putting this country in.

Madam Speaker, I just have two brief comments. I would note just in passing that prior to 1982, when my province's government was a New Democratic government, there were not deficits in Saskatchewan. Indeed, Saskatchewan was then a "have" province. Since 1982, with a Conservative government, it has had deficits and has become a "have not" province. Madam Speaker, on March 20 I asked the Minister of Agriculture if there would be financial assistance for Canadian farmers to enable them to plant their crops this year, and when that assistance would be forthcoming.
The minister responded that the government was working on this issue and was working with the provinces to design a program and that hopefully it would be a targeted program. As yet, not one penny of aid has reached the producers and, more than a month later, we are starting into the planting season.
I acknowledge that the government has give a commitment for $500 million of aid for Canadian farmers, but only if this amount is matched by the provinces. I understand that about $250 million of this goes to Saskatchewan, $100 million to Manitoba, $50 million to Alberta, $50 million for special crops and then $50 million for the rest of Canada.
While I do not quarrel with the division of funds, I have to wonder, for example, how the province of Manitoba can match its $100 million allotment when the total agriculture budget for the province is only $85 million. Many Manitoba farmers desperately need this help, as do farmers in other provinces.
I also have to wonder just how much good the $250 million is going to be to the Saskatchewan farmers, even if it is matched by the province, because the total of $500 million would mean $10 per acre planted in the coming season. We sincerely hope the recipients of this aid will be considered on a county-by-county basis and not on a basis that requires total townships or rural municipalities to be affected.
I have to remind the government that during the 1988 drought assistance program there were long waits for cheques and a lot of appeals. The farmers need this money now in order to purchase their crop input requirements. As I indicated earlier, planting has already started. Until the government announces what the assistance will be and shows how it is to be administered, the farmers will not even be able to get bridge financing pending the arrival of their assistance cheques.
I am fully aware that discussions are ongoing with the various provinces and producer groups and understand that some producer groups have suggested their payments be made through the Agricultural Stabilization Act and that the producer's sales records be used as the basis of those calculations. Such records, of course, are available from the various marketing boards or producer
April 23, 1990

organizations. I recognize that some of the producers who fed grain on the farm should also be compensated.
By comparison, it is totally unacceptable to Canadian farmers that producers in the United States receive half of their deficiency payments under their acreage allotment programs before they even plant their crops. In fact, they received this in the month of March. The other half of that payment will be made next year. In addition, they have a further advantage in that the input costs to the United States producers are 25 per cent less than those equivalent costs here in Canada. Consequently, our Canadian producers are at a distinct disadvantage, first, because they have no cash on hand to plant their crops and, second, their input cost are 25 per cent higher than those in the United States. Further delays simply cannot be tolerated.
I also like to place on the record that, while I do not disagree with the government's announcement of a few weeks ago to write down the debt of certain Caribbean countries due to their inability to repay, we have severe hardships here in Canada too. I respectfully ask the government to use Section ll(l)(e) of the Farm Credit Corporation Act and write down the debt load of some of our Canadian farmers who are being forced off their farms because this government has ignored the fact that these innocent victims of lower grain prices, which started to drop in the fall of 1984, need help too.
Under Section ll(l)(e) of that act, the government has the authority, under the objectives and powers of the act, to write down those loans, to make compositions, schemes of arrangements or to rewrite the mortgages itself.
Canada was built on the tradition of compassion and caring for the less fortunate. If there is ever a time to display some compassion and understanding, it is now. We have witnessed a tragedy after tragedy unfolding across this nation since last November. We have seen communities being devastated in Saskatchewan as people move away to seek work elsewhere. We have seen families being broken up and many people taking or attempting to take their own lives.
Adjournment Debate
I ask this government to acknowledge this and to take action to alleviate this worsening tragedy. If the government can write down debt for other countries, it should recognize the financial disaster unfolding in Canada and apply the same criteria here at home.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government does recognize what many Canadian farmers are going through a very tough and difficult time resulting from successive years of drought combined with uncertain prices and lingering debt.
I want to indicate as well that this government has responded in the past in many, many ways to help the agriculture industry of this country. We do not have to take a back seat to any country in the world in the support that we have given to our various sectors of agriculture.
When the Ministers of Agriculture met in Ottawa on March 29 and 30, the farm financial situation was the priority item on the agenda of that meeting. Unfortunately, in that short a time period the ministers could not come to an immediate agreement on how the federal government and the provinces could jointly address the problem. However, to send farmers and their creditors a clear signal of continuing support, the Minister of Agriculture announced a federal package of initiatives at the close of the ministers' meeting on March 30.
Under those initiatives the federal government will increase the flexibility of the farm debt review fund, which currently has $180 million available. The fund will be made more adaptable to current circumstances so that arrangements which farmers have worked out with the Farm Credit Corporation through the farm debt review process can be extended. That is responding to some of the special needs as well.
As well, the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds has asked the Canadian Wheat Board to implement procedures under the Prairie Grain Advance Payments Act, which should encourage creditors to extend needed operating credit to producers. This initiative will help to provide farmers with the several billion dollars in operating credit that they need this spring.

April 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate
We are also planning to extend the $150 million federal-provincial national soil conservation program. The additional $10 million we are willing to commit is contingent on provincial participation as well.
Once again, this government is prepared to dig deep to provide an additional $500 million in income assistance to our farmers. We are asking provincial governments to help their farmers by matching that federal contribution which alone would provide $1 billion more to Canadian farmers in the coming crop year and bring 1990-91 farm income in line with the five-year average.
We are willing to work quickly with the provinces to design the best approach for delivering assistance to producers. This initiative must be consistent with the policy pillars that underpin our current national agrifood policy review, namely, it must be production neutral, it must be environmentally responsible and it must lead us into a transition to a comprehensive long-term safety net.
As I said before, the government knows these are difficult times for Canadian farmers, but these are also financially difficult times for governments. It is not easy for any level of government to dig deeper. This includes the federal government as it struggles to control the huge national debt. About 35 cents of every federal tax dollar goes to service the federal debt compared with an average of 12 cents of every provincial tax dollar to service provincial debts. Yet total federal spending on agriculture in 1988-89 was almost two and half times of all provincial governments combined.
Still the Government of Canada stands ready and willing to come to the aid of farmers again this year. We are ready for further discussions with the provinces so that we can design programs that will be as comprehensive and effective as possible.

Madam Speaker, in answer to my question on April 9, 1990, concerning the government's aid package for the east coast fisheries, I was pleased to find that the Minister of Fisheries agreed with me when I asked him, as reported at page 10337 of Hansard:
Does the minister not think it would be wiser to be sure about the stocks and to be sure that we have fully developed all available species before we tell the people (on the east coast) that they must give up their life's work and the traditions of all those communities dependent on the fishery?
His answer in Hansard was one that I really agreed with. He said at page 10337:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I agree.
I was pleased because that seemed to signal, on the one hand, that the minister had been impressed by the arguments of so many fishermen in the southwestern end of Nova Scotia that these fishermen do not trust the department's stock assessment in the Scotia-Fundy region.
I was also pleased, on the other hand, that with his impending fisheries aid package he planned to greatly increase the department's participation in marketing the under-utilized species so that Atlantic Canadians could begin to reap the benefits of their total fish resource.
The reasons I have repeatedly asked both the minister and his predecessor to focus in the aid package for Nova Scotia on scientific evaluation and marketing are simple. First, to the best of my knowledge, there has never been any comprehensive stock assessment exercised in the Scotia-Fundy. Yes, research vessels have been sent out by the department, but for only a few weeks each year; two weeks on Brown's Bank and two weeks on George's Bank.
Local fishermen do not think this is enough to study the stocks. They think this because of what they are finding in the water. It does not bear out the department's pessimistic approach to stock evaluation. They will not go along with this with the exception of the haddock stocks which have been in a bad state since the early 1970s and are probably better today than they were then.
When I asked Dr. Leslie Harris in committee his opinion on the government's stock assessment on the Scotian shelf, he too felt that it was not good enough. The government has not yet applied the new "adapt model" to the Scotia-Fundy. This model has been used by the government to study the northern cod stocks since 1988 and, although it is not perfect, in the words of Dr. Harris, at least it would be a better evaluation than the hit and miss approach that the department is now taking.
April 23, 1990

Such an effort to evaluate the stocks might go some distance to repairing the non-existent credibility of the minister's department in this area, particularly in the Scotia-Fundy as it relates to stocks.
My second reason for being pleased was because the government has an equal responsibility to see to it that those affected by its poor management have a chance to profitably exploit the thousands of tonnes of so-called under-utilized species currently allocated to foreign boats within our 200-mile jurisdiction.
In this regard, the aid package should provide assistance to the fishermen and fish plant workers to go out after the under-utilized species and to market these species to the countries which come here to fish within our 200-mile jurisdiction and beyond. We have to put our money into establishing marketing of these under-utilized species. That means more money and considerably more money than the $1.9 million spent on all seafood promotion in Canada in 1989. This government will need to have in its aid package more money in that respect in order to fully develop on the east coast our under-utilized species and to compete with the foreigners who find it worth while to come here to fish, when we should be fishing.
I am not suggesting that this is a cure-all. I am just suggesting that we now have plants that are closed and boats tied up because they have been dependent on the three traditional stocks: cod, haddock and pollock. These plants and boats at present have no profitable alternative. I think one of the alternatives has to be with the under-utilized species and the markets that we could be searching for. At the same time that the minister brings out his aid package, I think the minister should listen to the fishermen and institute a uniform mesh size for not only the inshore but the offshore-those large, over 100-foot boats that are presently fishing and do not have any restriction on mesh size, and the foreigners who are fishing within our 200-mile limit who have no restriction on mesh size.
This regulation alone, if you listen to the inshore fishermen as to a mesh size, would probably conserve more fish than anything the minister could do in his aid package. I say that because in the last two weeks he has allowed the inshore 20,000 pounds of fish for three weeks, and he has allowed them to take it in cod,
Adjournment Debate
haddock or pollock. This means that they will go after the best fish and continue to dump. Had there been a mesh size for both the offshore-inshore foreigners, we would not have the dumping that is going on.
In closing, I asked my question in the spirit of offering advice that I thought would help the minister deal with the current crisis in a way that will lead to a positive solution and a healthy fishery for all. I do not like to see the negative approach which we have seen in the last few days which says that the minister criticizes the Atlantic Canadians for using the fishery, a renewable resource, as a point of entry into the unemployment insurance program. The fishery has been very profitable on the east cost. It is in a down period right now. We have alternatives. They are not to take away from the communities and the people who depend on the fisheries in those communities in the way that we heard from this minister last week.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this government is committed to an Atlantic fishery industry which is viable, productive and contributes significantly to the benefit of Atlantic Canadians. We recognize the importance of Canadians using our resources to the benefit of Canadians. Under-utilized species need to be utilized where they can. Sound conservation and management practices are the foundation on which all of this is built. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will soon be announcing a program for the Atlantic fisheries that will address current problems and permit us to move into ensuring a long-term viable industry.
Last year the government established an independent inquiry into the scientific and management aspects of the northern cod stocks following evidence of lower than anticipated growth in the biomass. The appointed panel examined data used in assessing and forecasting catches, the methodologies used in Canada and other countries, and the calculations leading to the 1989 assessment. The report by the Independent Review of the State of the Northern Cod Stock makes several recommendations on improving estimates of stocks, improving scientific research and expanding relevant technologies in the annual assessment process and in the management activities.
Similarly, the Scotia-Fundy Groundfish Task Force addressed a broad range of issues relating to the effec-

April 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate
tiveness of resource management, fleet capacity and the impact of adjustment. The task force makes several recommendations aimed at improving scientific evaluation. The task force also recommended improved conservation practices through methods such as improved regulations regarding gear size. All of these recommendations have been and will be discussed with the industry. We have already begun to implement the recommendations from these two reports and others are being explored in detail.
Both inshore and offshore harvesting sectors stand to gain from increased market penetration that can be realized through greater exploitation of under-utilized species. Of course, the processing sector will also benefit.
A pool of under-utilized groundfish was established as part of the 1990 Atlantic Groundfish Plan in order to increase the utilization of under-utilized fish stocks for the benefit of both harvesting and processing sectors. In addition, funds are being spent on under-utilized species under the federal-provincial fisheries subsidiary agreements. Also the Atlantic Fisheries Development Program, a Fisheries and Oceans program, funds work on the development of under-utilized species that are being caught at the present time. Some companies have already received allocations for the development of under-utilized species, particularly silver hake and mackerel.
The hon. member will know that this government has taken substantial action in this important area.

Madam Speaker, I rise today because I was totally unsatisfied with the minister's response to one of my questions about women's centre funding.
Before launching into my reasons why the Secretary of State's reply was unsatisfactory, I want to urge all ministers on the priorities and planning committee to positively answer the letters faxed to them by women's centre supporters in Newfoundland. The ministers have been asked whether they support the reinstatement of core funding for women's centres. It is a simple request, and a simple answer will do, a simple yes or a simple no. I
urge them to respond "yes" and to send their reply to the Newfoundland women as soon as possible.
I implore this government to take positive action concerning the women's centres. Stop wasting money on unnecessary security, spend it on core funding to the women's centres. Do not blow millions on Canada Day fireworks and celebrations, spend that money on women's centres. Let us have 10 minutes less of fireworks and fund our women's centres.
I want to specifically address the Secretary of State's reply to my question on April 10. My question was: Would the minister reinstate core funding for the women's centres? My point was the Secretary of State could spend about $560,000 on extra security for his regional offices. The Secretary of State was paying to fly women from Yukon, Newfoundland, British Columbia and Nova Scotia to Montreal to meet with him about funding. Why not spend that money on core funding for women's centres and eliminate this problem altogether?
The Secretary of State is now spending about one third of the budget cuts on an attempt at political damage control. Women are angry. Women are demonstrating because the funding for essential services has been cut. These women are not a threat. They are not violent women. They are simply protesting in the ways available to them, as citizens of a democratic country, their disagreement with this government's approach. Reinstate that funding and the Secretary of State would not need to hire extra security guards.
The minister did not bother to think about the impact of extra security on the Secretary of State's regional offices. Those offices also deal with citizenship applications for new Canadians. What are refugees to think? Refugees who may have escaped from police states, only to apply for citizenship in Canada, find locked doors and swarms of security guards preventing them from entering public offices. Secretary of State offices are public buildings. The minister should know that something is deeply wrong when he decides that he must lock the offices from the public-the ones who pay for these offices.
The Secretary of State did not respond to my question on April 10. He simply attempted to turn it around and ask me if I thought he should not be meeting with women from the women's centres. Well he would not have to waste half a million dollars on security and on flying people around the country if he would simply
April 23, 1990

reinstate the core funding. He just did not have an adequate answer to my question.
The women from the centres just want their funding back so that they can continue to provide the information, referral and the counselling services that are essential to their communities and to the women in those communities.
I have spoken out many times, both here in the House and outside on the issue of funding for women's centres. On the particular day in question, busloads of women from Quebec came here to lobby for their women's centres. My colleague, the member for Chambly, Quebec, shared the question with me that day on women's funding. He is also very concerned about the abdication of federal responsibility toward women's centres as are all New Democrats. He mentioned that 39 out of the 75 centres completely cut off core funding are Quebec women centres. That is more than half the women centres cut. He questioned the Secretary of State's press secretary for saying that the federal cut had "a beneficial effect" on Quebec women's centres.
The press secretary tried to make it sound like Quebec's decision to increase funding for women's centres happened as a result of the federal budget and these cuts. In fact, that decision was made last summer. The Quebec government has been counting on the federal government's core funding. The extra funding was to supplement, not to replace federal funding. The Quebec government official that we spoke to that morning said that the federal budget could not be called by any stretch of the imagination beneficial to women. The Quebec government has recognized the value and the necessity of women's centres. Obviously this federal government has not.
In my own province of British Columbia women's centres are closing their doors. They are shutting down. They cannot continue to operate without core funding. Ten women's centres in British Columbia have already had to close because of this Tory government. It seems that the word "Tory" has come to be synonymous with bad news for women in Canada.
In response to the question of the member for Chambly, the Secretary of State replied how pleasant his meetings were with the women involved. They would be a sight more pleasant if he would guarantee the core
Adjournment Debate
funding to women's centres. Again the Secretary of State appears to be a master of avoiding the question. He did not give the member for Chambly a reply to his specific question, nor did he give me a real response to my question. My question, as taken from Hansard of April 10, 1990, was:
Will the Secretary of State reinstate the core funding to women's
programming and will he do it today?.
Since the minister did not answer yes or no, I am anxious to hear from his representative today. Will women's centres, the ones which have been shut, be allowed to reopen? Will the core funding be reinstituted for women's programming? Will it be done today? Yes or no?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House to respond to the hon. member's question of April 10 regarding a Secretary of State meeting with representatives from women's centres.
My hon. colleague was critical that the minister was spending money to bring women to Montreal for a meeting in light of the cuts the government has made to the core funding for women's centres.
I am sure that if the hon. member gave it some additional thought she would acknowledge that during these difficult times of financial restraint, communication between government and Canadians is of utmost importance.
By having representatives from several women's centres all together, a useful dialogue was able to take place between the minister, his officials and the concerned representatives of the women's centres.
The minister was realistic at the meeting. He did not pretend that he was about to give the women all the answers they wanted to hear. But it was an excellent opportunity for the women to voice their concerns. It was an equally good opportunity for the minister to explain the situation his department and the government find themselves in.
Although core funding to women's centres has been discontinued, the government did not take that decision lightly. It is part of the sacrifice that all Canadians are being asked to make in order to get our financial house in order.

April 23, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Reducing the deficit and controlling spending are absolutely essential if we hope to build a healthy and competitive economy, an economy which will enable us to implement social programs and support social vehicles such as women's centres.
Only that kind of economy can create a social climate that will nourish true equality for women and Canadians.
The funding reductions to the women's program have been a difficult decision to make but I ask my hon. colleague to remember that during this fiscal year the women's programs will support more than 500 projects.
As the minister and other government members have pointed out the women's centres are being encouraged to apply for project funding. The minister has assured
them that they will receive administrative funding for specific projects.
That is what the minister was able to explain to the women he met in Montreal. There was no illusion that everyone would go away fully satisfied, but communication is essential during these difficult times and an important exchange of ideas and opinions took place at that meeting.
